title: Until Spring
passages:
Wren pulled the deck light off its lanyard and raked it out over the starboard shoulder, and the beam found her ten meters off in the trough: face-down, one arm thrown up over her head, the catch bag riding high beside her, still clipped to her wrist, dragging her sideways every time the sea leaned.

"Nia," she said into comms, flat, because shouting at water only costs you your voice. "Nia Vos."

The arm moved. Not a stroke. A hand opening.

"She's alive," Wren said. "I think she's alive."

"Think harder," Sol said.

Dey had both fists on the rail and the mast-step lashing still around his waist, and he hauled at it twice, the way a dog tests a chain it already knows the length of. "Cut me loose."

"You can't lift that bag, never mind her," Wren said. "Your scrubber's shot. You go in, we fish out two bodies and one of them's stupid."

"Say it kinder."

"No time to be kind twice."

Behind her the drum ticked as it cooled. Bayo stood at it with his right forearm laid over the brake pin, because that was the only part of him still working; the bandage on his left hand had gone the color of rust and was weeping through in two places, and he looked at it the way you look at a tool somebody else broke.

"Bayo," Sol said. "Can you take her weight."

"No." Fast and clear, and Wren's head came round, because in fourteen months she had never once heard him give a straight no. "Not on a line, not with these. I'd have her up in pieces. I'm telling you now instead of after." He opened his fingers and the wrap made a small wet sound. "Somebody else's hands. Mine are finished, and I'm not cutting anything tonight just to keep from saying so."

"Well," Sol said. "That's new."

Salas was already stripping the spare harness off the rail hook. Gray to the lips, fourteen months of air pocket still sitting behind his eyes, and his fingers worked the webbing without any trouble at all.

"No," Sol said, and her hand went to the red mushroom on the drum housing, the emergency stop that killed the winch and set the brake in one motion; she kept it there the way other people keep a knife. "Mara's recording was clear. Nobody already hollowed goes below the Line."

"This is above it. The Line's a depth, Captain, not a mood." He clipped the safety line to his own harness, twenty meters of floating line, the kind that rides on top instead of sinking on you. "I'm not asking for the drum. I go in, I clip her, you bring us both up. I only ever need to know which side the air's on, and I've never lost that yet."

"You'll forget the way back."

"Then don't let me swim it."

Wren counted three sets under her breath. "Twelve seconds between slams. Eight to work, four to get flat and take it on your back. You're still in the water on the eleventh second, you're under the hull, and the hull doesn't care who you are."

"Eight," Salas said. "I've had eight."

She threw him the second light. He caught it one-handed and put it in his teeth.

"Line's yours, not his," Sol told Bayo. "You can hold a slack line sitting down."

"I can hold a slack line," Bayo agreed, and got his forearms over it.

Sol looked at Salas a moment longer, then took her hand off the stop, which was as close as she came to permission. "Over on nine. Back on the rail by twenty-one, or I haul up whatever's on the end."

"Generous."

"It isn't."

He went over on nine. The sea took him at the shoulders and turned him once, and the floating line came off the coil hissing. Wren lay flat with the light in both hands and tracked the pale of him against the black of the hull. Seven. Eight. His hand closed on Nia's harness at the shoulder and stopped, because the ascent line still trailed off her waist, looped over on itself and snagged on something under her, and every slam drew it tighter.

Wren had time to think, quite clearly, *he's going to make this and I am not editing one second of it.*

Then the light on the gate tower overhead flipped from red to amber.

Nobody had to explain amber. Under the hull, deep and grinding, the shutter motor came awake, and the Kettle began closing itself one tooth at a time.

"Salas," Sol said. "*Eight seconds.*"
